correctness.rationale: The well-defined Carathéodory scalar Green-Ampt ODE has a nonincreasing capacity and a 1-Lipschitz-in-rainfall flux. In the high-flow coordinate the low-flow speed ratio is nondecreasing, giving the exact flow derivative w(Psi_v(z))/w(z) >= 1. Strictness is exactly crossing the interval (F_h,F_l) where this ratio grows; because before F_h both rates penetrate entirely, this yields the stated two necessary and sufficient inequalities. Adjacent swaps and the L1 contraction of both infiltration solutions and scalar rearrangements give the bounded-measurable extension. Analytic root solving and 3000 seeded parameter checks reproduce examples but are not used as infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The two fully inspected Green-Ampt literature treatments develop redistribution and numerical rainfall models rather than prove a histogram-extremal final-infiltration law and a two-intensity strict iff boundary for the immediate-runoff scalar equation. The 1978 Chu and 1993 Philip articles have only abstracts accessible here. General monotone-flow interchange principles may furnish an independent derivation, so novelty is narrowly limited to this hydrological exact combination under explicit assumptions and remains open to independent checking.
residual_risks: Philip (1993) and Chu (1978) mathematical bodies inaccessible; an explicit or implied ordering lemma may appear there.
A broad scalar flow rearrangement theorem might imply the weak bound even if hydrology papers do not mention it; the two-rate exact boundary is the narrower claim.
Physical models with surface water storage, runoff recapture, redistribution and soil heterogeneity need not satisfy the theorem.
Independent scientific audit and comprehensive literature review have not been performed.

value.rationale: Provides a global upper and lower envelope on effective infiltration and runoff given only a finite-horizon rainfall intensity histogram and fixed Green-Ampt capacity parameters, without optimizing over schedules numerically. The sharp necessary-and-sufficient two-bin thresholds distinguish when temporal rearrangement changes the hydrological prediction and when nonlinear capacity has no effect. The scope is scientifically motivated by storm shape and runoff response, not a selected artificial integer or textbook single-step computation; explicit physical assumptions and no-redirection limits constrain its application.
